And that's it!  🎉 GPT-3 correctly reverses long words! But to get there, we had to teach GPT-3 the algorithm to use to get around its limitations. 💪 https://t.co/Gy4nP52ytr

GPT-3 has trouble removing the spaces and merging tokens.

You can teach it to break down the task into steps. In each step, you remove every other space: "a l p h a b e t" becomes "al ph ab et", which becomes "alph abet", and finally "alphabet".
So close! It manages to reverse the letter sequence, but fails at removing the spaces in the last step. It's the tokenization striking again.

We can teach it to order characters by having it add numbers to keep track of the letters in the sequence.
 
This simple trick makes the ordering explicit, and GPT-3 now manages to reverse the letters correctly. https://t.co/BqW8AA6AsM

But it's still not great at reversing words, because it gets "confused" by the ordering in long sequences.

This is the second reason GPT-3 is bad at reversing words. https://t.co/ESkcSg3w2I
We can make GPT-3 "see" the letters by having it add spaces between them. Then each letter becomes its own token: " a", " l", " p" and so on. https://t.co/KHxbREaCGm
Tokens are chunks of characters. For example, the word “alphabet” gets broken up into the tokens “alph" and "abet”. Short and common words like “the” are a single token.
The first reason GPT-3 is bad at reversing words is due to tokenization: it doesn't see letters and words as humans do. Instead, it sees "tokens."

@OpenAI In the end, this result is not so much about the Rubik's Cube, as it is about learning dexterity as step towards general purpose robots. The techniques are quite general: RL + ADR could in principle be applied to any task you can simulate.

@OpenAI Another surprising side-effect of using ADR with a recurrent neural network, was the emergence of meta-learning. Our hypothesis is that the network learns to both solve the task and figure out the properties of the environment it's in (the real world) at the same time. 8/n
@OpenAI One anecdote was that during the filming, one of the fingers of the robot broke, but we didn't notice for over an hour since the robot still kept solving the cube. 7/n

@OpenAI The network is also surprisingly robust. We messed with the robot quite a bit: occluding cameras, put on a rubber glove, tied the fingers. And it still does a fairly solid job at solving the cube. 6/n

@OpenAI The strategies the neural network policy learns are often suprising, but once you see them make a lot of sense. For example, the hand uses its little finger much more than a human, but its little finger is also abnormally big. 5/n
@OpenAI For example, modeling friction of cubelets, springiness, etc would be really hard to figure out best randomizations for. 4/n
@OpenAI This lead us to automatic domain randomization (ADR). ADR removed a ton of manual work to set randomizations, which would have been super tricky with Rubik's cube. 3/n
@OpenAI It's been suprising to me how well sim2real works with RL + domain randomization. The biggest obstacle we faced was to set randomization ranges as complexity of the environment increased. 2/n
Excited to share what we've been working on at @OpenAI Robotics for the past year: we used RL and a new technique called automatic domain randomization to train a robot to solve Rubik's Cube. 1/n
